parole.testo: Borrowed from German dunkel, from Proto-Germanic *dunkalaz. Cognate with Old Norse døkkr.

parole.significato: a larger, relatively flat piece, especially an ice floe; a floe, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed through German flach (“flat”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *flakaz.
Borrowed from German Forelle, from Proto-Germanic *furhnō. The fish is spotted, hence the name. Compare Sanskrit पृषत् (pṛṣat, “spotted”), Ancient Greek περκνός (perknós), πέρκη (pérkē).
Borrowed from German kleben, from Proto-Germanic *klibāną.

parole.significato: to make (something) less (physically or emotionally) painful; to relieve, to alleviate, to ease
parole.testo: From German lindern, from German lind (“mild”), from Proto-Germanic *linþaz.
From German Luder (“carcass used as bait, hussy”), from Proto-Germanic *lōþr-.
Borrowed from German Meißel, from Old High German meizil, from Proto-Germanic *maitilaz.
From German Morchel, from Middle High German morchel, from Old High German morhila, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *murhǭ.

parole.significato: public (open or available to the public)
parole.testo: From German öffentlich, from Middle High German offen, Old High German offan, ofan, ophan, from Proto-Germanic *upanaz. Cognate with Swedish öppen.
Borrowed from German Schnitz, from schnitzen, from Proto-Germanic *snittōną. Attested since 1888. Doublet of schnitzel, sned, snida, and snitt.

parole.significato: a stalk (stem or main axis of a plant)
parole.testo: From German Stengel, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stangilaz, equivalent to stång (“pole”) + -el (“diminutive suffix”).

parole.significato: passion, craze, mania, enthusiasm (warm enthusiasm for something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Wurm (“worm”), from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz. Doublet of orm. In folklore, a person with a particular whim or fancy had worms in their head. Compare English maggot (“a whimsy or fancy”). See also German Bücherwurm, English bookworm.
